paper_title: OmniVerifier-C1: Decomposed Graded Verifier for Rule-Governed Generative World Modeling

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Generative visual verifiers play a crucial role in advancing multimodal intelligence. To enhance the robustness of visual verifiers in complex multimodal scenarios involving compositional requirements, we move beyond conventional binary verifiers that produce only True/False discrete judgments and introduce a verifier that automatically decomposes complex prompts or environmental rules into fine-grained components and assigns pointwise scores to provide a continuous and more informative critique signal. Our experiments further demonstrate that these structured and interpretable outputs improve the verifier's generalization to out-of-domain multimodal critic tasks. To train this verifier, we introduce a Decoupled RL training strategy that jointly optimizes sub-question-level binary judgment and global alignment scoring, using precise local feedback to develop fine-grained verification capabilities that provide a foundation for reliable continuous scoring at the global level. Under a general reinforcement learning framework, we first empirically demonstrate that the proposed pointwise graded verifier significantly outperforms binary verifiers in traditional text-to-image scenarios. We then extend our investigation to rule-governed generative world modeling where generative models are leveraged for world simulation and world reasoning under explicit rules. From a theoretical standpoint, we further show that a pairwise verification paradigm yields more accurate critiques than the pointwise formulation when ground-truth images are available, with empirical results on diverse structured world-modeling tasks such as Maze and Sudoku further validating the effectiveness of our approach. Overall, our findings suggest a key insight: the transition from generative models to structured world-modeling agents critically hinges on the availability of accurate pairwise graded visual verifiers.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Multimodal generative models have made remarkable progress in recent years (Cao et al., 2025; Seedream et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026), producing visually compelling images conditioned on textual descriptions. Beyond visual fidelity (Wiedemer et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2024b; Yang et al., 2025b), central challenge lies in whether generated images faithfully follow complex instructions and reflect coherent world knowledge (Zhou et al., 2025; Jin et al., 2026; Deng et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2025a; Huang et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026b). Motivated by this challenge, visual verifiers have emerged as crucial component for assessing the correctness of generated results. By providing feedback on the alignment between images and textual descriptions, verifiers not only serve as evaluation tools, but also act as general critic models for inferencetime scaling and reinforcement learning-based training. As generative models are increasingly applied to open-ended environments and reasoning-intensive tasks, the reliability and expressiveness of visual verifiers become key bottleneck for advancing multimodal intelligence. Despite their importance, most existing visual verifiers (Zhang et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2025a; Xiong et al., 2025) adopt binary judgment paradigm that produces only True/False decisions about whether an image satisfies given prompt. Although simple and efficient, this design has several inherent limitations. First, binary supervision provides coarse feedback that fails to capture the partial correctness of generated samples. By assigning the same negative label to imperfect samples of varying quality, binary rewards obscure meaningful quality differences and weaken the within-group learning signals required by group-relative reinforcement learning. Moreover, the limited information conveyed by binary labels may encourage shortcut learning and increase susceptibility to reward hacking (Shao et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026c), as models may exploit superficial patterns to predict the expected labels without adequately reasoning about the subtl compositional relationships among objects, attributes, and spatial constraints. To address these limitations, we propose the Decomposed Graded Verifier (OmniVerifier-C1), which automatically decomposes complex prompts or environmental rules into fine-grained sub-questions and performs structured reasoning over each component. It assigns continuous scores based on the proportion of satisfied sub-questions, capturing partial correctness and providing informative critique signals. Our experiments demonstrate that decomposition-based structured reasoning significantly improves the verifiers out-of-domain multimodal critic capabilities. To train this verifier, we introduce Decoupled RL training strategy that jointly optimizes sub-question-level binary judgment and global alignment scoring, using precise 0/1 feedback on individual sub-questions to develop strong fine-grained verification capabilities that support reliable global scoring. Moreover, our theoretical analysis shows that the decompositionand-scoring paradigm better preserves the underlying true quality ordering among generated samples, providing finer-grained learning signals for group-relative reinforcement learning. Building upon this verifier, we further explore its role as generative reward model for reinforcement learning across two types of tasks. First, we apply the verifier to traditional text-to-image alignment, where it provides fine-grained feedback that encourages generative models to satisfy detailed compositional relationship. Second, we extend our study to the more reasoning-intensive and challenging setting of structured generative world modeling, where generative models are used to simulate environments and reason over sequential states. In these rule-governed environments, we find that pairwise verification, which compares generated states against ground-truth states, provides more accurate and reliable critiques than pointwise verification. This observation suggests that the effectiveness of visual verification in rulegoverned world-modeling scenarios critically depends on the availability of reference states for comparison. Extensive experiments across diverse tasks, such as Maze and Sudoku, demonstrate that the proposed verifier provides more reliable reward signals and substantially improves reinforcement learning performance. Our contributions can be summarized as follows: We propose the Decomposed Graded Verifier, which automatically decomposes complex prompts or environmental rules into fine-grained sub-questions, performs structured reasoning over each component, and assigns continuous scores based on the proportion of satisfied sub-questions. Our experiments demonstrate that its structured outputs significantly improve out-of-domain multimodal critic capabilities. OmniVerifier-C1: Decomposed Graded Verifier for Rule-Governed Generative World Modeling We introduce Decoupled RL training strategy that jointly optimizes sub-question-level binary judgment and global alignment scoring, using precise 0/1 feedback on individual sub-questions to develop fine-grained verification capabilities that provide foundation for reliable scoring. We demonstrate that the proposed verifier serves as an effective generative reward model for reinforcement learning, improving performance in both traditional text-to-image generation and rule-governed generative world modeling tasks. We provide empirical validation across diverse structured reasoning environments, showing that accurate pairwise decomposed verifiers are key enabler for transforming generative models into rule-governed world-modeling agents.

sections.title: 3.1 Theoretical Advantage of Decomposed Graded Rewards for Generative RL
sections.content: Drawbacks of Binary Reward. Binary verifiers have emerged as an effective tool for improving text-toimage generation quality through inference-time scaling (Zhang et al., 2025b). When they detect semantic inconsistencies between generated image and its textual description, they produce editing instructions that guide the generative model to iteratively refine the visual output. For this purpose, coarse binary feedback is often sufficient, as the verifier primarily serves as gating mechanism that determines whether further refinement is needed. However, binary verifiers face inherent limitations when used as reward models for reinforcement learning, as their feedback is insufficiently dense and discriminative to distinguish among imperfect samples of varying visual quality and thereby guide effective generative policy optimization. Revisiting Decomposition-Based Continuous Rewards. To address this limitation, we introduce the Decomposed Graded Verifier, structured verification paradigm that elicits continuous scores from visual verifiers. Instead of reducing assessment to single binary judgment, it decomposes complex prompt into fine-grained sub-questions, evaluates each sub-question individually with binary judgments, and aggregates these local decisions into continuous score that reflects the degree of prompt satisfaction. sections.title: 3.2 Graded Verification Enhances Multimodal Reasoning and Critique Capabilities
sections.content: Drawbacks of Binary Outcome Supervision. Binary verifiers supervise model training solely through the final True/False outcome, implicitly assuming that correct verdict reflects correct reasoning process. This assumption is often reasonable in domains such as mathematical problem solving, where the solution space is large and arriving at the correct answer typically requires coherent multi-step reasoning. However, it becomes much more fragile in binary multimodal critique tasks. Without explicit supervision over the judgment process, verifier may exploit shallow visual patterns or shortcut cues to produce seemingly correct verdicts without genuinely understanding the underlying multimodal reasoning process (Wang et al., 2026c; Shao et al., 2025), thereby leading to reward hacking Experiment Setup. We collect textual prompts from ShareGPT-4o-Image (Chen et al., 2025) and control prompt length to construct samples with varying levels of complexity. To enhance visual diversity, we randomly sample from multiple generative models, including FLUX.1-dev (Labs et al., 2025), Qwen-Image (Wu et al., 2025), and Z-Image (Team, 2025b), to generate the corresponding images. We then perform supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to learn the sub-question decomposition paradigm distilled from Seed1.8 (Seed, 2026). Using the SFT-trained model, we filter out samples whose predictions exactly match the ground truth, and further apply GPT-5 (OpenAI, 2025a) Bo10 filtering strategy to remove samples with accuracy below 60% while controlling the proportion of fully correct samples at 30%. The remaining high-quality samples are used for Decoupled Reinforcement Learning with DAPO (Yu et al., 2025) on Qwen3-VL-8B (Team, 2025a). The model is trained for 80 steps on 16 NVIDIA A800-80G GPUs and evaluated on ViVerBench (Zhang et al., 2025b). Decoupled Reinforcement Learning. As shown in Fig. 2, given textual prompt and its corresponding generated image y, we convert each pair into + 1 reinforcement learning samples, where denotes the number of decomposed sub-questions. Specifically, one sample is used for decomposition-based continuous OmniVerifier-C1: Decomposed Graded Verifier for Rule-Governed Generative World Modeling scoring policy optimization, while the remaining samples are used for binary fine-grained judgment policy optimization. For the decomposition-based scoring sample, the verifier takes the textual prompt and the generated image as input, and is trained to predict the global alignment score induced by the decomposition. Given the predicted score ˆS [0, 1] and the ground-truth score [0, 1], the reward is defined as Rscore = 1 ˆS S. For each fine-grained judgment sample, the verifier takes the k-th sub-question Qk and the generated image as input, and is trained to predict the binary answer associated with this sub-question. Given the predicted answer ˆAk {0, 1} and the ground-truth answer {0, 1}, the reward is defined as Rjudgment = 1[ ˆAk = k]. During reinforcement learning, we mix these two types of samples and optimize them with their respective rewards, forming decoupled RL training scheme that jointly optimizes sub-question-level binary judgment and global alignment scoring. Precise 0/1 feedback on individual sub-questions enables the verifier to develop fine-grained verification capabilities that provide foundation for reliable continuous scoring. Experiment Analysis. Table 1 shows that the Decomposed Graded Verifier achieves stronger generalization than the Discrete Binary Verifier on ViVerBench, comprehensive and challenging benchmark for evaluating multimodal reasoning and critique. Notably, the Decomposed Graded Verifier requires supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to learn the structured decomposition paradigm. By contrast, the Discrete Binary Verifier only needs to produce binary True/False verdict with corresponding textual explanation, and can therefore be directly optimized through reinforcement learning. For fair comparison, we evaluate the Discrete Binary Verifier in both RL-only and SFT+RL settings. The results show that the Discrete Binary Verifier consistently underperforms the Decomposed Graded Verifier, regardless of whether it is first adapted with SFT. This indicates that the key factor is not the training pipeline itself, but the nature of the supervision signal. Binary supervision is highly compressed and sparse, which encourages the model to rely on shallow patterns rather than capturing complex semantic structures. In contrast, the Decomposed Graded Verifier decomposes complex tasks into multiple sub-questions and performs finegrained judgments, thereby explicitly enforcing structured reasoning process. This mechanism provides richer and more informative feedback signals, effectively mitigating reward hacking and substantially improving the models multimodal reasoning and critique capabilities. Moreover, our Decoupled RL training strategy jointly optimizes sub-question-level binary judgment and global alignment scoring, using precise 0/1 feedback on individual sub-questions to strengthen fine-grained verification capabilities and thereby provide foundation for robust generalization to out-of-distribution (OOD) scenarios.

sections.title: 4 Verifier-Guided Reinforcement Learning for Generative Models
sections.content: In this section, we investigate how the Decomposed Graded Verifier guides generative model optimization through reinforcement learning. We begin with traditional text-to-image generation task, and then focus on studying how to adapt the verifier to provide more reliable reward signals for rule-governed world modeling scenarios.

sections.title: 4.2 Verifier-Guided RL for Rule-Governed World Modeling
sections.content: Traditional text-to-image generation primarily targets semantic alignment, where prompt may admit multiple diverse and visually plausible outputs, leaving no well-defined unique ground-truth image. By contrast, world simulation and reasoning tasks are rule-governed and highly structured, where the desired final state is often uniquely determined by the initial state and the underlying rules, thereby making OmniVerifier-C1: Decomposed Graded Verifier for Rule-Governed Generative World Modeling Figure 3: Qualitative visualization of traditional text-to-image generation. ground-truth image available in many scenarios. Motivated by this property, we explicitly introduce the ground-truth image as an additional visual input to the verifier, which simplifies the verification process and enables the verifier to produce more accurate and reliable reward signals for rule-governed generative world modeling. Formally, given an initial visual state and rule-based instruction c, the generative model πθ is required to understand the underlying rules and perform rule-governed reasoning to produce resulting image πθ(y x, c) , which can be viewed as visual prediction of the target final state. Similar to the traditional text-to-image setting, the instruction can be decomposed into fine-grained sub-questions = {q1, q2, . . . , qK}, each assessing whether the resulting image satisfies specific sub-rule or achieves corresponding sub-goal. sections.title: 5 Experiments
sections.content: In this section, we conduct comprehensive experiments to demonstrate the advantages of the Decomposed Graded Verifier as generative reward model and the superiority of the pairwise verification mechanism in rule-governed world modeling scenarios.

sections.content: Training Datasets. For traditional text-to-image tasks, we use textual prompts from ShareGPT-4oImage (Chen et al., 2025), the same data source used for verifier training. For rule-governed world modeling scenarios, we construct six game-based tasks to comprehensively evaluate generative models abilities in path planning, logical reasoning, geometric construction, pattern induction, character recognition, and spatial reasoning . sections.content: Graded Rewards Are Better than Binary Rewards. The Decomposed Graded Verifier consistently achieves superior performance, demonstrating that fine-grained graded reward signals are more effective for improving the semantic alignment capability of generative models. Fig. 3 further supports this conclusion through qualitative visualizations. Fig. 1 (a)(b) shows the training dynamics under the two reward models. We evaluate intermediate checkpoints every 10 steps on held-out set of 500 textual prompts under the same decomposition-based scoring protocol, using Gemini3.1-Pro (Google DeepMind, 2026) as an evaluator not involved in data processing. Compared with the Discrete Binary Verifier, training with the Decomposed Graded Verifier yields steadier and more pronounced performance improvements, suggesting that denser and more discriminative rewards support more stable and effective optimization. Comparison with Other Continuous Reward Models. We compare the Decomposed Graded Verifier with UnifiedReward (Wang et al., 2025b), which also focuses on semantic alignment and produces continuous reward scores. As shown in Table 2, our method achieves superior performance on both GenEval (Ghosh et al., 2023) and CLIPScore (Hessel et al., 2021), supporting the ability of the Decomposed Graded Verifier trained with our Decoupled RL strategy to provide more accurate and fine-grained reward signals and highlighting its advantages as generative reward model.

From Easy-to-Hard and Domain Generalization. To more comprehensively evaluate the generalization potential of the model trained with pairwise verification, we construct more challenging Hard Dataset that is excluded from training. This dataset contains larger-scale instances and compositional tasks designed to test reasoning in more complex structured environments. As shown in Table 3 and Fig. 4, the model exhibits strong performance across out-of-distribution scenarios, including shifts in the visual domain. These results suggest that the model acquires transferable capabilities for structured reasoning and rule-governed world modeling beyond task-specific training patterns, highlighting the advantages of pairwise verification in supporting robust generalization. Since Qwen-Image-Edit2509 has not been specifically trained on game-based image-to-image generation tasks, it often fails to interpret the required transformation. In practice, the model tends to either the model tends to either leave the input image unchanged or distort its original structure, indicating that it lacks the task-specific action priors required for this domain. After supervised fine-tuning on our constructed game-based dataset, the generative model learns the visual style of these tasks and the corresponding rule-based transformation patterns. Although the model still often fails to produce fully correct solutions, it begins to perform meaningful operations toward the desired final state rather than generating irrelevant or destructive visual outputs, leading to clear performance improvements. These results indicate that SFT primarily equips the model with domain-specific execution ability, while subsequent reinforcement learning further endows the generative model with reasoning intelligence. In both multimodal understanding and generation Generative Intelligence Beyond the Text Encoder. models, the text encoder is often regarded as the primary source of reasoning intelligence. For generative OmniVerifier-C1: Decomposed Graded Verifier for Rule-Governed Generative World Modeling models, this view implies that the text encoder interprets instructions and provides semantic guidance, while the DiT primarily executes the visual generation process. However, in our training pipeline, the text encoder remains frozen throughout both SFT and RL, and only the DiT parameters are updated. The reasoning capabilities observed after training suggest that reasoning intelligence is not encoded exclusively in the text encoder, as the DiT can also learn, internalize, and express capabilities for structured reasoning and rule-governed world modeling.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: This work introduces the Decomposed Graded Verifier as an effective reward model for improving visual generation in both traditional text-to-image tasks and structured world-modeling scenarios. Our contributions are twofold. First, we propose Decoupled RL training strategy that jointly optimizes subquestion-level binary judgment and global alignment scoring, using precise local feedback to develop fine-grained verification capabilities that support accurate continuous scoring. Empirical results further demonstrate improved out-of-domain multimodal critic capabilities. Second, focusing on rule-governed world modeling, we introduce pairwise verification paradigm that explicitly incorporates ground-truth images as visual references. This simplifies verification by shifting from reason-then-judge process to direct reference-based comparison, thereby producing more accurate and reliable reward signals. Extensive experiments validate the effectiveness of both the Decomposed Graded Verifier trained with our Decoupled RL strategy and the pairwise verification paradigm. Therefore, reward model that better preserves the true quality ordering also provides more reliable relative policy updates. The decomposed graded reward is strictly monotonic with respect to the number of satisfied sub-questions and thus preserves all pairwise quality comparisons. sections.content: B.1 Training Dynamics across Six Game-Based Tasks Fig. 5 presents the training dynamics of pairwise and pointwise verification across our six constructed rulegoverned tasks. Following the evaluation protocol in the main text, we evaluate intermediate checkpoints every 10 training steps on the corresponding validation sets, using Gemini3.1-Pro (Google DeepMind, 2026) as an evaluator not involved in data processing and providing ground-truth images as explicit references. Across all six tasks, pairwise verification generally yields more sustained performance improvements and higher final scores, whereas pointwise verification exhibits more pronounced fluctuations and limited progress. This trend is consistent with the aggregate results in the main text. By directly comparing generated outputs with ground-truth references, pairwise verification reduces reliance on internal targetstate inference and can provide more reliable reward signals for policy optimization. These results further support the effectiveness of reference-based verification across different types of rule-governed visual generation tasks. Figure 5: Training dynamics of pairwise and pointwise verification across six rule-governed tasks. Each panel shows validation scores and the score gap between the two methods. B.2 Sub-question-level Verification Accuracy The reliability of decomposed graded scoring depends on whether the verifier correctly judges individual sub-questions against the generated image. Even when the decomposition is appropriate, incorrect local judgments can introduce noise into the aggregated reward. We therefore directly evaluate sub-question-level verification accuracy on held-out set of 200 binary sub-question samples. Three authors and two Ph.D. students each annotate 40 samples, collectively providing human labels for all 200 samples. We additionally OmniVerifier-C1: Decomposed Graded Verifier for Rule-Governed Generative World Modeling obtain binary annotations from GPT-5.5 and Gemini-3.1-Pro on the same evaluation set. Excessive decomposition can introduce redundant questions or requirements unsupported by the original prompt. For example, given red apple is placed on table, the verifier may repeatedly ask whether an apple exists or introduce questions such as Is the apple fruit? and Is the apple round? that do not correspond to explicitly requested visual constraints. Such questions can distort the aggregated score by repeatedly weighting the same requirement or introducing irrelevant criteria. We also observe that generating more sub-questions can lead to violations of the required output format, reducing the reliability of the final score. Together, these observations highlight the importance of balancing fine-grained coverage with faithful and non-redundant decomposition.

sections.title: C Limitations and Future Works
sections.content: Our world-modeling evaluation is restricted to game-based environments with explicit rules, where the ground-truth image is uniquely determined by the initial task state and rule instructions. We adopt these controlled tasks primarily to evaluate the effectiveness of our pairwise verification paradigm. Although our results demonstrate the advantages of pairwise verification in these settings, these tasks capture only part of the complexity and diversity of real-world environments. In future work, we plan to extend our investigation to open-ended settings with non-unique ground truths, construct larger and more realistic world-modeling datasets, and scale both the verifier and the generator to stronger backbones. Our long-term goal is to develop multimodal generative models that can reason about, simulate, and interact with complex real-world scenes.
